result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_node()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get a node object by ID or label. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L6385-L6466){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_node(node) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Get node](/assets/graphs/get-node.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph with node ids in pills. Node B, the query, is outlined in the accent color with its id 2 highlighted. The card returns the Node object Node(id=2, label='B')." width="100%"} Retrieves the `Node` object for the specified node. The `Node` object has three properties: `id` (the integer node ID), `label` (the string label, or `None` if the node has no label), and `attributes` (a dict of the node's attributes, including `type` if one was set, or `None` if the node has no attributes). This is the quickest way to inspect everything stored on a single node, for example when debugging how a graph was built or reading a few attributes inside a loop. To look at many nodes at once, `get_node_df()` returns all of them as a table. How a missing node is handled depends on how it was referred to: an integer ID that doesn't exist returns `None`, while a label that doesn't exist raises a `ValueError`. The `attributes` dict is not a copy: changing it changes the attributes stored in the graph, so treat it as read-only and use `set_node_attrs()` for deliberate changes. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to retrieve, given either as its integer node ID or as its string label. An `int` is always treated as an ID and a `str` always as a label, so `"2"` looks for a node labelled `"2"`, not the node with ID `2`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Node | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `Node` object, or `None` if `node=` is an integer ID that isn't in the graph. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is a label that doesn't match any node. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is neither an `int` nor a `str`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `get_node()` accepts either a label or an internal ID, and returns the underlying `Node` object with its `id`, `label`, and `attributes`: ::: {#c02758d1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_node(label="A", color="red", size=10).add_node(label="B") node = graph.get_node("A") node.id ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: The label is tracked separately from the auto-assigned ID: ::: {#ff458ca6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} node.label ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 'A' ``` ::: ::: Any extra keyword arguments passed to `add_node()` are stored in `attributes`: ::: {#49ff344d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} node.attributes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'color': 'red', 'size': 10} ``` ::: ::: Passing an integer looks the node up by ID instead. Node `"B"` was added second, so it has ID `2`: ::: {#42f24e95 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Node(id=2, label='B') ``` ::: ::: An ID that isn't in the graph returns `None`, which makes it easy to test for existence: ::: {#04a8201b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node(99) is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: :::
